reasoning: The work accepted was, in its own words, "to make the grader treat that extra act as a failure instead" — so the shift in which recorded runs count as passing is the very thing ordered, not something the delivery added on its own. The document settles this case directly: "A redefinition he ordered himself is not that third case: he settled the fork when he ordered it, and carrying out his decision is executing it, not making it." The converse clause is what would have moved it: "where a delivered change reaches past what he ordered and redefines behaviour he never named, that wider half is the third case." Nothing here reaches past — the four runs turning red are the ordered rule applied to the runs it was ordered to judge, with no second redefinition of correctness beyond the extra-act rule he named. The delivered state also fails none of the closing bars: "Nothing is broken, and the code does what the instruction said," its own unit tests pass, so this is not "a red check" or an unmet scope under "A task cannot close while its accepted scope still holds todo/target/not-built, a missing artifact, or a red check" — the 26/35 is the graded corpus reading under the new rule, not a failing acceptance command. The lower score is therefore a result to be shown, not a gate: "A shown result closes the work; the human's own eye is never the gate on an ordinary delivery... It never leaves a row open to wait for the human to look at what was already shown and bless it." Should he then object to the four newly-red runs, "that disagreement is a new fact, not a reopening of the one that shipped: it becomes its own task carrying his correction, and the closed row stays closed." Nothing here is irreversible outside git, so rule 12's stop-before-running clause does not bite.
